Abnormality of the lung parenchyma extending to the pulmonary interstitium and leading to diffuse pulmonary fibrosis.
An increased susceptibility to pneumonia as manifested by a history of recurrent episodes of pneumonia.
A recurrent hemorrhage occurring within the lung.
Obstruction of conducting airways of the lung.
An increased susceptibility to bronchopulmonary infections as manifested by a history of recurrent bronchopulmonary infections.
A type of pulmonary sequestration that is completely enclosed in its own pleural sac, occurring above, within, or below the diaphragm, and without communication with the tracheobronchial tree.

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation, a condition most commonly associated with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, is an abnormal communication between the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein without an intervening capillary communication. HRCT images usually show a coarse spidery appearance of the peripheral vascular markings in the lungs. More specific findings are obtained in the pulmonary angiogram where the normally invisible capillary phase is replaced by irregular vascular channels bridging the peripheral branches of pulmonary arteries and veins.

Hepatic failure refers to the inability of the liver to perform its normal synthetic and metabolic functions, which can result in coagulopathy and alteration in the mental status of a previously healthy individual. Hepatic failure is defined as acute if there is onset of encephalopathy within 8 weeks of the onset of symptoms in a patient with a previously healthy liver.
A diffuse form of hepatic steatosis.
Decreased activity of complex III of the mitochondrion in the liver.
The presence of abnormal calcium deposition in the liver.
Hyperplasia of the biliary tree, as manifested by increased size of bile ducts, dilated lumen, and histologically by an increased number of epithelial cells or hyperplasia.
Inflammation of the liver due to infection with a virus.
Intermittently increased size of the liver.
An abnormal increase in the amount of intracellular lipid droplets in hepatocytes.
An increase in the amount of glycogen stored in hepatocytes compared to normal.
The presence of reduced numbers of intrahepatic bile duct than normal.
An acute form of hepatic steatosis.
A type of cirrhosis characterized by the presence of large regenerative nodules.

Neonatal jaundice refers to a yellowing of the skin and other tissues of a newborn infant as a result of increased concentrations of bilirubin in the blood. Neonatal jaundice affects over half of all newborns to some extent in the first week of life. Prolonged neonatal jaundice is said to be present if the jaundice persists for longer than 14 days in term infants and 21 days in preterm infants.
Fibroblast proliferation and fiber expansion from the portal areas to the lobule.
An abnormal reduction in the number of mitochondria in hepatocytes.
Repeated occurrences of acute noninflammatory encephalopathy and fatty degenerative liver failure.

The two portions of the clavicle (corresponding to the two primary ossification centers of the clavicle) are connected by a fibrous bridge that is contiguous with the periosteum, and a synovial membrane develops, resulting in a clavicle with a bipartite appearance radiographically. Congenital pseudarthrosis of the clavicle generally presents as a painless mass or swelling over the clavicle.
An abnormally straight configuration of the clavicle, a tubular bone which normally is doubly curved .
Lack of development of the glenoid fossa, also known as the glenoid cavity, which is the articular surface of the scapula that articulates with the head of the humerus.
Bony fusion between the humerus and scapula, leading to an impairment in mobility of the affected shoulder joint.
The presence of a paralyzed diaphragm.
Irregular surface of the normally relatively smooth border between the distal part of the ribs and the costal cartilages, which are bars of hyaline cartilage that connect the ribs to the sternum.
Early ossification of the costochondral junction, which is the joint between the ribs and costal cartilage in the front of the rib cage.
Underdevelopment of the middle portion of the clavicle.
A larger than usual distance between the left and right nipple.

A less than normal number of sternal ossification centers. The sternum is initially formed from bilateral sternal plates that chondrify and begin to fuse with ribs at 10 weeks gestational age. Ossification starts in the manubrium and upper part of the sternal body at the 6th month, in the middle of the sternal body at the 7th month, in the lower part of the body during the 1st postnatal year and in the xiphoid process between years 5 and 18. The number of ossification centers vary up to six, and it is the ossification centers that are visualized by prenatal ultrasound. This term describes a reduction in the number of ossification centers compared with age-related norms.
Lack of formation and mineralization of the ribs in utero.
Deposition of calcium salts in point-like foci within the anterior portion of one or more ribs.
Abnormal increase in density of the tissue at the costochondral junctions.
Breast carcinoma that is bilateral or otherwise multifocal.
Lack of formation of mineralized bony tissue of the sternum.
Underdevelopment of the glenoid fossa, which is the cavity in the lateral part of the scapula which articulates with the head of the humerus.
Osteosclerosis of ribs (increased density related to increased bone mass).
Developmental defect resulting in congenital absence of the middle portion of the clavicle.

More than one fracture of the ribs. Callus formation around multiple rib fractures can produce a row of multiple rounded expansions (beadlike prominences) giving the appearance of beaded ribs. Note that rachitic rosary would have one bead per rib (a swelling at the costochondral junction), while beaded ribs in the context of multiple rib fractures have multiple beads (fractures) along the same rib.
Abnormally reduced diameter (cross section) of the clavicles.

Calcification of the costal cartilages, which are bars of hyaline cartilage found at the anterior ends of the ribs which serve to prolong the ribs forward and contribute to the elasticity of the walls of the thorax.
Chest wall pain in the area of the costochondral junctions.
Absence of the clavicles as a developmental defect.
An abnormal morphology of the ribs consisting of shorted, abnormally curved ribs. On posteroanterior chest radiography, the ribs show a curvature resembling that of a coat hanger (clothes hanger).
Increased time for the complex comprised of the Q wave, R wave, and S wave as measured by the electrocardiogram (EKG).. In adults, normal values are 0.06 - 0.10 sec.

Inflammation of the coronary arteries involving a granulomatous response, i.e., a non-specific inflammatory response involving granulomas, defined as a compact organized collection of mature mononuclear phagocytes including epithelioid and giant cells.

Premature ventricular contractions (PVC) or ventricular extrasystoles are premature contractions of the heart that arise in response to an impulse in the ventricles rather than the normal impulse from the sinoatrial (SA) node.
An abnormality of filling of a ventricle with blood during diastole.
A form of ventricular preexcitation due to the presence of multiple accessory pathways for cardiac conduction.
The presence of excessive connective tissue in the endocardium.
Abnormal tortuous (i.e., twisted) form of the aorta.
A bacterial infection of the endocardium, the inner layer of the heart, which usually involves the heart valves.
A benign tumor of connective tissue containing mucous or gelatinous material (myxoma) localized in the pumonic valve.
Abnormally short chordae tendineae of the tricuspid valve.
A defect of the atrioventricular septum of the heart.
A localized outpouching of ventricular cavity that is generally associated with dyskinesia and paradoxical expansion during systole.
A type of cardiac arrhythmia with premature atrial contractions or beats caused by signals originating from ectopic atrial sites.
Acute occurrence of a dissection (tear within the tunica intima and entry of blood into the tunica media) of a coronary artery.
Any structural abnormality of the coronary arteries.
An abnormality of an atrioventricular valve.
An abnormality of the hepatic vasculature.
Absence or underdevelopment of the clavicles (collar bones).
A form of acute leukemia characterized by excess lympoblasts.
The presence of an adenocarcinoma of the pancreas.
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia of T-cell origin. It comprises about 15% of childhood cases and 25% of adult cases. It is more common in males than females.

A paraganglioma (previously referred to as chemodectoma) located in the retroperitoneal space. Paragangliomas (also known as extra-adrenal pheochromocytomas) are rare tumors that arise from extra-adrenal chromaffin cells. Paragangliomas are characterized by secretions of excessive catecholamines, including epinephrine, norepinephrine and dopamine, which may lead to clinical symptoms, including episodic hypertension, tachycardia and diaphoresis. However, between 40 and 50% of paragangliomas are non-functional.
The presence of an follicular adenocarcinoma of the thyroid gland.
A type of papillary renal cell carcinoma in which the papillae are covered by large eosinophilic cells with pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and nuclear pseudostratification.
A rare subtype of acute myeloid leukemia evolving from primitive megakaryoblasts.
The presence of an adenoma in the cortex of the kidney.
Pheochromocytoma not originating from the adrenal medulla but from another source such as from chromaffin cells in or about sympathetic ganglia.
Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin is a malignant tumor of squamous epithelium.
The presence of a carcinoma of the urinary bladder with origin in a transitional epithelial cell.
A malignant neoplasm of the adrenal cortex that may produce hormones such as cortisol, aldosterone, estrogen, or testosterone.
Pheochromocytoma originating from the adrenal medulla.
A neurofibroma (benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor) localized adjacent to the spine.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the stomach.
The presence of leiomyosarcoma of the skin.
The presence of a malignant neoplasm of the genital system.
The presence of a carcinoma in the renal pelvis.
A slowly growing malignant neoplasm derived from cartilage cells.
The presence of renal cell carcinoma in the renal papilla.

A type of pituitary adenoma originating in prolactin secreting cells. This kind of adenoma is characterized by overproduction of prolactin, and may cause loss of menstrual periods and breast milk production in women.
A subtype of renal cell carcinoma thought to originate from mature renal tubular cells in the proximal tubule of the nehpron.
A malignant epithelial tumor with a glandular organization that originates in the duodenum.
A benign renal neoplasm composed of fat, vascular, and smooth muscle elements.
The presence of a papillary adenocarcinoma of the ovary.
A malignant plasma cell tumor growing within soft tissue or within the skeleton.
A non-malignant neoplasm of the genitourinary system.
A malignancy of the parathyroid glands. Parathyroid carcinoma usually secretes parathyroid hormone, leading to hyperparathyroidism.
A kind of thyroid adenoma characterized by the presence of oxyphil cells.
Muscular dystrophy affecting the muscles of the limb girdle (the hips and shoulders).
Any anomaly of the anterior horn cell.
Perceptual experiences that are vivid, intense, and sensory in nature occur in the absence of corresponding stimuli from the external environment.
Reduced amount of myelin in the nervous system resulting from defective myelinogenesis in the white matter of the central nervous system.
An anomaly of the white matter of the brain localized in the region posterior to the cerebral ventricles.
A type of focal clonic seizure characterized by sustained rhythmic jerking rapidly involves one side of the body at seizure onset.
Absence or underdevelopment of the vermis of cerebellum.

A form of lissencephaly in which the cortex is thickened and has four more or less disorganized layers rather than six normal layers resulting from incomplete neuronal migration during brain development. At neuropathological examination, a 4-layered cortex consists of an upper molecular layer, a second thin cellular layer containing pyramidal neurons usually observed in layer V, a third pale poorly cellular layer and a fourth thick deep layer made up of neurons which had failed to migrate. Radiologocally would manifest as agyria or pachygyria with cortical thickness greater than 10 mm.
A type of polymicrogyria with a gradient of severity (anterior more severe than posterior) extending from frontal poles posteriorly to precentral gyrus and inferiorly to frontal operculum.
An abnormally pale appearance of the dorsal portion of the gray substance of the spinal cord. This finding can be observed by histological examination.
A severe degree of muscular hypotonia characterized by markedly reduced muscle tone.
A cessation of the development of a child in the areas of motor skills, speech and language, cognitive skills, and social and/or emotional skills, following the onset of epilepsy.
A type of Horner syndrome with congenital onset.
Absence of the knee jerk reflex, which can normally be elicited by tapping the patellar tendon with a reflex hammer just below the patella.
Developmental defect characterized by a small and malformed corpus callosum.
Underdevelopment of the ventral portion of the pons.
Multiple neurofibromas of the spinal nerve roots with a symmetric distribution.
The occurrence of repeated episodes of generalized muscular hypotonia.
Wasting (atrophy) of the vermis of cerebellum.
A loss or impairment of the sensation of the relative position of parts of the body and joint position occurring at distal joints.
A severe delay in the acquisition of the ability to use language to communicate needs, wishes, or thoughts.

A type of holoprosencephaly in which most of the right and left cerebral hemispheres and lateral ventricles are separated but the most rostral aspect of the telencephalon, the frontal lobes, are fused, especially ventrally.
A symmetric and progressive loss of myelin from the internode regions along myelinated nerve fibers of the peripheral nervous system.
Atrophy affecting the pons and the cerebellum.
A diffuse loss of myelin from the internode regions along myelinated nerve fibers of the peripheral nervous system.
A decrease in the ability to perceive vibration in the distal portions of the limbs.
Borderline intellectual disability is defined as an intelligence quotient (IQ) in the range of 70-85.
Atrophy (wasting, decrease in size of cells or tissue) affecting the frontotemporal cerebrum.
Hallucinations occurring during the transition from sleep to wakefulness.

Malfunction of the abducens nerve as manifested by impairment of the ability of the affected eye to be moved outward. Patients who develop abducens nerve palsy often present with binocular horizontal diplopia, which is a double vision when looking at objects side by side. There will be a notable weakness of the ipsilateral lateral rectus muscle leading to a deficit in of eye abduction on the affected side. Some patients may present with a constant head turning movement to maintain binocular fusion and to lessen the degree of diplopia.
The presence of calcium deposition within brain structures that is present already at the time of birth.
Curvilinear intracellular accumulation of autofluorescent lipopigment storage material within axons.
Stiffness (a condition in which muscles cannot be moved quickly without accompanying pain or spasm) of the axial musculature.
Excessive number of small gyri (convolutions) on the surface of one side of the brain.

Brain damage related to a lowering of blood glucose below a critical level (around 30 mg/dl), which may lead to confusion, lethargy and delirium followed by seizures and coma. Prolonged hypoglycemia may lead to irreversible brain damage.
The presence of developmental dysplasia of the cortex of frontal lobe and the cortex of parietal lobe.
Pericallosal lipomas are congenital soft masses of adipose cells encapsulated by a thin layer of fibrous tissue, appearing adjacent to the corpus callosum of the brain.

Relatively short-lived periods of psychosis are characterized by the sudden onset of severe disturbances in perception, thinking, and behavior. These episodes typically last for a brief duration, generally ranging from a few days to a few weeks, and are often triggered by a significant stressor or traumatic event.
Nystagmus dating from or present at birth.

A reduced sense of touch (tactile sensation) on the skin of the distal limbs. This is usually tested with a wisp of cotton or a fine camel's hair brush, by asking patients to say 'now' each time they feel the stimulus.
A decrease in the ability to perceive vibration at the ankles. Clinically, this is usually tested with a tuning fork which vibrates at 128 Hz and is applied to the malleoli of the ankles.
A complete loss of the ability to perceive vibration.
An increased susceptibility to meningitis as manifested by a medical history of recurrent episodes of meningitis.
Hypoplasia of the cerebellum, pontine nuclei, and inferior olivary nucleus.

An abnormality of the auditory evoked potentials, which are used to trace the signal generated by a sound, from the cochlear nerve, through the lateral lemniscus, to the medial geniculate nucleus, and to the cortex.
Proximal spinal muscular atrophy, i.e., muscular weakness and atrophy related to loss of the motor neurons of the spinal cord and brainstem.
The presence of calcium deposition in the choroid plexus.

Periventricular leukomalacia is characterized by diffuse injury of deep cerebral white matter, accompanied in its most severe form by focal necrosis. The neuropathologic hallmarks of PVL are microglial activation and focal and diffuse periventricular depletion of premyelinating oligodendroglia.
A type of encephalopathy (brain disease, damage, or malfunction accompanied by an altered mental state) that is characterized by evidence of necrosis of brain tissue.
Deficit in grammar, including syntax and morphology.
Any abnormality of an individual's circadian rhythm that affects the timing of sleeping and being awake is referred to as a sleep-wake disorder.
Leukoencephalopathy that gets more severe with time.
A type of holoprosencephaly characterized by the presence of a single ventricle and no separation of the cerebral hemisphere. The single midline ventricle is often greatly enlarged.

Dysplasia and dysgenesis of the corpus callosum are nonspecific descriptions that imply defective development of the corpus callosum. The term dysplasia is applied when the morphology of the corpus callosum is altered as a congenital trait. For instance, the corpus callosum may be hump-shaped, kinked, or a striped corpus callosum that lacks an anatomically distinct genu and splenium.
A type of gliosis that occurs in the vicinity of injured neurons.
Focal proliferation of glial cells in the basal ganglia.

Progressive impairment of function of motor axons with muscle weakness, atrophy, and cramps. The deficits are length-dependent, meaning that muscles innervated by the longest nerves are affected first, so that for instance the arms are affected at a later age than the onset of deficits involving the lower leg.
The formation of small cavities in the tissue of the basal ganglia.

An abnormality of the ability (skills) to perform a precise movement of small muscles with the intent to perform a specific act. Fine motor skills are required to mediate movements of the wrists, hands, fingers, feet, and toes.

Paralysis of the fourth cranial (trochlear) nerve manifested as weakness of the superior oblique muscle which causes vertical diplopia that is maximal when the affected eye is adducted and directed inferiorly.

An abnormality of the ability (skills) to perform a precise movement of large muscles with the intent to perform a specific act. Gross motor skills are required to mediate movements of the arms, legs, and other large body parts.

Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) manifests at age 2-3 years or by first grade at the latest. The main symptoms are distractibility, impulsivity, hyperactivity, and often trouble organizing tasks and projects, difficulty going to sleep, and social problems from being aggressive, loud, or impatient.
Cerebral hemorrhage that occurs before birth.

Bilateral impairment of the function of the cranial nerves 9-12, which control musculature involved in eating, swallowing, and speech. Pseudobulbar paralysis is characterized clinically by dysarthria, dysphonia, and dysphagia with bifacial paralysis, and may be accompanied by Pseudobulbar behavioral symptoms such as enforced crying and laughing.
A morphological abnormality of the metencephalon.
A small, sac-like aneurysm (outpouching) of a cerebral blood vessel.

Cerebellar dysplasia (abnormal growth or development) is defined by abnormal cerebellar foliation, white matter arborization, and gray-white matter junction. Cerebellar dysplasia is a neuroimaging finding that describes abnormalities of both the cerebellar cortex and white matter and is associated with variable neurodevelopmental outcome. Dysplasia may globally involve the cerebellum or affect only one cerebellar hemisphere. In addition, cerebellar dysplasia may be associated with cortical/subcortical cysts.
A type of congenital malformation in which brain tissue protrudes through a defect in the anterior (front) part of the skull.

A symmetric magnetic resonance imaing (MRI) abnormality of the basal ganglia characterized by an increase of signal intensity in T2-weighted images and a corresponding signal decrease on T1-weighted images.
Meningitis that persists for more than 4 weeks, and lymphocytes are present in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
Partial or complete wasting (loss) of dentate nucleus.
Increased size of the basal ganglia.
Hyperactive stretch reflexes of muscles that move proximal joints (elbow, knee).
Generalized atrophy or hypoplasia of the cerebrum.
Progressive loss of previously present language abilities.
Stiffness of the limbs (a condition in which muscles cannot be moved quickly without accompanying pain or spasm) occurring in the proximal limb muscle.
Peripheral sensory neuropathy affecting primarily distal sensation.
Underdevelopment of the inferior portion of the vermis of cerebellum.
Increased vertical dimension of the corpus callosum. This feature can be visualized by sagittal sections on magnetic resonance tomography imaging of the brain.
Muscular rigidity (continuous contraction of muscles with constant resistance to passive movement).
A reduction in the amplitude of sensory nerve action potential. This feature is measured by nerve conduction studies.
An increase in size of the third ventricle.
Fasciculations affecting the tongue muscle and the musculature of the face.
Episodes of choreoathetosis that can occur following triggers such as quick voluntary movements.

Arnold-Chiari type I malformation refers to a relatively mild degree of herniation of the posteroinferior region of the cerebellum (the cerebellar tonsils) into the cervical canal with little or no displacement of the fourth ventricle. It is characterized by one or both pointed (not rounded) cerebellar tonsils that project 5 mm below the foramen magnum, measured by a line drawn from the basion to the opisthion (McRae Line)
A darker than expected signal on magnetic resonance imaging emanating from the cerebral white matter.
Encephalopathy with onset in the infantile period.
A loss of myelin from the internode regions along myelinated nerve fibers from segments of the peripheral nervous system.
Demyelinating neuropathy is characterized by slow nerve conduction velocities with reduced amplitudes of sensory/motor nerve conduction and prolonged distal latencies.
A type of encephalocele that occurs along the medial orbit wall at the level of the frontal process of the maxilla and the ethmoid-lacrimal bone junction.
A particular type of dementia characterized by a pattern of mental defects consisting prominently of forgetfulness, slowness of thought processes, and personality or mood change.
Amyotrophy (muscular atrophy) affecting the proximal musculature.
Acute progressive areflexic weakness and mild sensory changes resulting from myelin breakdown and axonal degeneration.
Neurodegeneration involving the globus pallidus,a part of the basal ganglia that is involved in the regulation of voluntary movement.
Muscular atrophy of distal arm muscles.
Stiffness of the limbs (a condition in which muscles cannot be moved quickly without accompanying pain or spasm) occurring in an asymmetric pattern.
A progressive degree of muscular rigidity (continuous contraction of muscles with constant resistance to passive movement).
Changes in one's level of awareness and responsiveness to their environment.
A diffuse loss of myelin from nerve fibers in the central nervous system.

A form of gray matter heterotopia were the mislocalized gray matter is typically located periventricularly, also sometimes called subependymal heterotopia. Periventricular means beside the ventricles. This is by far the most common location for heterotopia. Subependymal heterotopia present in a wide array of variations. There can be a small single node or a large number of nodes, can exist on either or both sides of the brain at any point along the higher ventricle margins, can be small or large, single or multiple, and can form a small node or a large wavy or curved mass.
Episodic bouts of involuntary movements with dystonic, choreic, ballistic movements, or a combination thereof. There is no loss of consciousness during the attacks.
A complete lack of the ability to track objects with the ocular smooth pursuit system, a class of rather slow eye movements that minimizes retinal target motion.

Atrophy of the interosseus muscles (including the palmar interossei that lie on the anterior aspect of the metacarpals, the dorsal interosseus muscles of the hand, which lie between the intercarpals, the plantar interosseus muscles, which lie underneath the metatarsal bones, and the dorsal interossei, which are located between the metatarsal bones.
Reduced amount of myelin in the nervous system resulting from defective myelinogenesis in the peripheral nervous system.
A lighter than expected T2 signal on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the basal ganglia. This term refers to a localized hyperintensity affecting a particular region of the basal ganglia.

Loss of awareness of oneself or one's surroundings, involving (i) a loss of normal motor control is evident as flaccidity or stiffness, either of which can be accompanied by jerking movements, and postural control is lost so that patients fall if they are in an upright position; (ii) normal responsiveness is lost; and (iii) the patient experiences amnesia for the event. Loss of consciousness my be transitory (e.g., syncope) or prolonged.
A congenital absence of the convolutions of the cerebral cortex and a poorly formed sylvian fissure that affects a particular part of the cortex.
Facial diplegia (that is, bilateral facial palsy) with congenital onset.
Bilateral tonic-clonic seizure of either generalized or focal onset occurring on or soon after wakening (typically within 90 minutes of waking, regardless of the time of day).
Recurrent episodes of hypersomnia (sleeping 16 or more hours a day) over a period of days or weeks.
The formation of the formation of fibrofatty lesions in the wall of an artery located in the brain.
Enlargement of all or parts of one cerebral hemisphere.
Generalized-onset tonic-clonic seizures that are provoked by flashing or flickering light.
Presence of irregular redundant loops of focally folded myelin in a peripheral nerve.
Complete loss of ability to move facial muscles innervated by the facial nerve (i.e., the seventh cranial nerve).
Muscular atrophy affecting the lower limb.
Episodes of muscle weakness associated with elevated levels of potassium in the blood.
The presence of calcium deposition in the cerebral white matter surrounding the cerebral ventricles.
A reduction in the amplitude of sensory nerve action potential in distal nerve segments. This feature is measured by nerve conduction studies.
Groups of small caliber axons in peripheral nerve biospies indicative of axonal regeneration.
A type of gait ataxia displaying progression of clinical severity.
Alternating and recurrent weakness of the external ocular muscles.
Functional neurological abnormalities related to dysfunction of the pyramidal tract.
A severe loss of myelin from nerve fibers in the central nervous system.
A form of lissencephaly characterized by an uneven cortical surface with a so called 'cobblestone' appearace. There are no distinguishable cortical layers.
A symmetric loss of myelin from the internode regions along myelinated nerve fibers of the peripheral nervous system.
Atrophy affecting the cerebellum and the spinocerebellar tracts of the spinal cord.
Defective structure and function of myelin sheaths of the white matter of the brain.
An abnormality characterized by chronic impairment of the normal functioning of the axons.
Muscular weakness and atrophy related to loss of the motor neurons of the spinal cord and brainstem.

An atypical absence seizure is a type of generalized non-motor (absence) seizure characterized by interruption of ongoing activities and reduced responsiveness. In comparison to a typical absence seizure, changes in tone may be more pronounced, onset and/or cessation may be less abrupt, and the duration of the ictus and post-ictal recovery may be longer. Although not always available, an EEG often demonstrates slow (<3 Hz), irregular, generalized spike-wave activity.
An increased susceptibility to bacterial meningitis as manifested by a medical history of recurrent episodes of bacterial meningitis.
A cessation of the development of a child in the areas of motor skills, speech and language, cognitive skills, and social and/or emotional skills.
Paralysis of the facial nerves on the basis of overgrowth of the cranial bones causing impingement upon the seventh cranial nerve.
Nystagmus consisting of horizontal to-and-fro eye movements, in which the movement in one direction is faster than in the other.
Fasciculations affecting the musculature of the arms and legs.
A discrete posterior fossa cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) collection that does not communicate directly with the fourth ventricle.

Oral-motor apraxia is the inability to volitionally sequence oral movements of the speech structure for nonspeech tasks in the absence of neuromuscular deficits such as paralysis or muscle weakness. Oral-motor apraxia is diagnosed when, despite intact sensory motor function an individual is unable to use these effector systems under voluntary control.
Bipolar disorder is an illness of mood characterized by alternating episodes of elevated and depressed moods, which are interspersed with euthymic periods.
A loss of myelin from nerve fibers in the central nervous system.

Loss of neurological function in a time frame that is considered relatively quick, for instance, loss of a develomental milestone or substantial exacerbation of neurological complications such as seizures or feeding difficulties within a few months.
Multiple areas of darker than expected signal on magnetic resonance imaging emanating from the deep cerebral white matter.
A type of dystonia that affects all or most of the body.
Reduced ability to perceive painful stimuli.

A type of anterior encephalocele in which there is a protrusion of the contents of the skull through a breach at the point where the frontal and ethmoidal bones meet. Frontoethmoidal encephalocele can be divided further into three distinct categories: nasofrontal, nasoethmoidal, and nasoorbital.
Focal seizure characterized at onset by clonic movements affecting half of the face.
Underdevelopment of the frontal lobe of the cerebrum.
A bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with focal onset is a focal-onset seizure which progresses into a bilateral tonic-clonic phase.
Recurrent episodes of brain dysfunction that may be triggered by factors such as metabolic disturbances or infections.
A saccade that overshoots the target with the dynamic saccade.
Weakness of the muscles of the legs.

Any structural anomaly of the limbic system, a set of midline structures surrounding the brainstem of the mammalian brain, originally described anatomically, e.g., hippocampal formation, amygdala, hypothalamus, cingulate cortex. Although the original designation was anatomical, the limbic system has come to be associated with the system in the brain subserving emotional functions. As such, it is very poorly defined and doesn't correspond closely to the anatomical meaning any longer. [BirnLex].
Increased intensity of the a reflex in the arm.
A type of tremors that is triggered by holding an arm in a fixed position.

A focal-onset seizure is a type of seizure originating within networks limited to one hemisphere. They may be discretely localized or more widely distributed, and may originate in subcortical structures.
A structural abnormality of the pons.
The presence of atrophy (wasting) of the cerebrum, also known as the telencephalon, the largest and most highly developed part of the human brain.
Absence or underdevelopment of the corpus callosum.
The presence of atrophy (wasting) of the corpus callosum.
An abnormality of the septum pellucidum, which is a thin, triangular, vertical membrane separating the lateral ventricles of the brain.
An abnormality of the choroid plexus, which is the area in the cerebral ventricles in which cerebrospinal fluid is produced by modified ependymal cells.

An abnormality of somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEP), i.e., of the electrical signals of sensation going from the body to the brain in response to a defined stimulus. Recording electrodes are placed over the scalp, spine, and peripheral nerves proximal to the stimulation site. Clinical studies generally use electrical stimulation of peripheral nerves to elicit potentials. SSEP testing determines whether peripheral sensory nerves are able to transmit sensory information like pain, temperature, and touch to the brain. Abnormal SSEPs can result from dysfunction at the level of the peripheral nerve, plexus, spinal root, spinal cord, brain stem, thalamocortical projections, or primary somatosensory cortex.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the gastrointestinal tract.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the genitourinary system.
Telangiectases (small dilated blood vessels) located near the surface of the skin of the face.
A developmental defect resulting in the congenital absence of skin on the scalp.
A type of ichthyosiform erythroderma with postnatal onset.
Photosensitivity of the skin occurring early in life.
Developmental hypoplasia of the apocrine sweat glands in the region of the axilla.
A nonspecific term denoting wasting, especially as a result of degeneration, of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and neurosensory retinal cells in the macula.
Abnormal thickening of the skin on the palms and soles charactersized by hyperkeratosis of the stratum corneum with no evidence of epidermolysis characteristic of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis.
Increased susceptibility to infection by the protozan parasite of the genus Leishmania.
An abnormally increased perspiration on palms and soles.
Naevus flammeus localized in the skin of the forehead.

Cutaneous lesion that develops as a dry, scaly, red patch that evolves to an indurated and hyperpigmented plaque with adherent scale. Scarring may result in central white patches (loss of pigmentation) and skin atrophy.
Spontaneous development of hematomas (hematoma) or bruises without significant trauma.
Telangiectases (small dilated blood vessels) located near the surface of the skin of the cheeks.
Telangiectasia (that is, the presence of small dilated superficial blood vessels) of the oral mucosa.
The presence of two to five cafe-au-lait macules.
Generalized abnormal accumulation of fluid beneath the skin, or in one or more cavities of the body.
An ichthyosiform abnormality of the skin with congenital onset.
Hemangioma is a benign tumor of the vascular endothelial cells. This term refers to facial hemangiomas that have a plaque-like morphology.
The presence of multiple leiomyomas of the skin.
Absence of melanin pigment in various areas, which is found at birth and is permanent. The lesions are known as leucoderma and are often found on the face, trunk, or limbs.
A type of blistering that affects the skin of the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet.
Diffuse abnormal thickening of the skin on the palms and soles.
Inability to sweat on the same side of the face that is affected by ptosis and miosis. This is a feature of Horner syndrome.
Lichenification affecting primarily flexural areas of the skin.
The spontaneous detachment of a digit (finger or toe) from the body due to long standing pathology.
Keratinization of the bulbar conjunctiva near the limbus (corneoscleral junction), resulting in a raised spot.
Reduced number or density of facial hair.
Abnormal thickening of the skin on the palms and soles with an honeycomb pattern.
Increased amount of keratin (visible as white scales) surrounding hair follicles.
Cutis gyrata of palms and soles.
Subcutaneous nodules that are located in the vicinity of joints.

An ichthyosiform abnormality of the skin that presents at birth or shortly thereafter with generalized erythema, blistering, erosions, and peeling. In the subsequent months, erythema and blistering improves but patients go on to develop hyperkeratotic scaling that is especially prominent along the joint flexures, neck, hands and feet.
An abnormality of dermatoglyphs (fingerprints), which are present on fingers, palms, toes, and soles.

The term collodion baby applies to newborns who appear to have an extra layer of skin (known as a collodion membrane) that has a collodion-like quality. It is a descriptive term, not a specific diagnosis or disorder (as such, it is a syndrome). Affected babies are born in a collodion membrane, a shiny waxy outer layer to the skin. This is shed 10-14 days after birth, revealing the main symptom of the disease, extensive scaling of the skin caused by hyperkeratosis. With increasing age, the scaling tends to be concentrated around joints in areas such as the groin, the armpits, the inside of the elbow and the neck. The scales often tile the skin and may resemble fish scales.
Telangiectases (small dilated blood vessels) with a diffuse localization.
Hyperkeratosis affecting the palm of the hand and the sole of the foot in areas exposed to friction.
Increased susceptibility to staphylococcal infections, as manifested by recurrent episodes of staphylococcal infections.
The presence of fewer than normal sweat glands.

A skin condition characterized by excessive development of keratin in hair follicles, resulting in rough, cone-shaped, elevated papules resulting from closure of hair follicles with a white plug of sebum.
Tiny bumps of thickened skin (hyperkeratosis) on the palms of the hands.
An abnormal accumulation of fluid beneath the skin on the back of the hands.
Loose and sagging skin of the fingers.
Loose, wrinkled skin of hands and feet.
Loss of hair in the occipital region of the scalp with congenital onset.
A severe degree of photosensitivity of the skin.
Presence of a cutaneous lipoma on the forehead.
Lack of skin pigmentation (coloring) of the anterior chest.

Congenital large depigmented (white) macule of irergular rhomboid shape. Piebald skin depigmentation generally presents with multiple such macules in the affected individual. There may be smaller (5-15mm), discrete, skin-colored and hyperpigmented macules interspersed within the depigmented macules.
Abnormal thickening of the skin on the palms and soles that is present at birth.
Hyperkeratosis affecting the sole of the foot.
The presence of six or more cafe-au-lait spots.
Seborrheic dermatitis that is not localized to any one particular region.

Hyperkeratosis lenticularis perstans (HLP), also known as Flegel disease, is a keratinization abnormality characterized by small, asymptomatic erythematous papules that leave characteristic punctate bleeding when they become detached. The lesions generally occur symmetrically along the top of the foot and on the legs, appearing more rarely on the arms, forearms, palms, and soles, and even on the oral mucosa.
A form of atopic dermatitis with onset in adulthood characterized by atopic red face, chronic lichenified eczema on the trunk, subacute or psoriasiform dermatitis.
A neurofibroma (benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor) localized in the palm of the hand.
Increased pigmentation of the skin with a netlike (reticular) pattern.
A developmental defect resulting in the congenital absence of skin on the trunk or the limbs.
Absence or developmental hypoplasia of the eccrine sweat glands.
The presence of multiple subcutaneous lipoma that cause pain.
The distal and proximal transverse palmar creases are merged into a single transverse palmar crease on both hands.
An abnormal accumulation of fluid beneath the skin, or in one or more cavities of the body because of decreased osmotic pressure of plasma (hypoproteinemia).
Naevus flammeus localized in the skin of the neck. This is one of the most common birthmarks and present in approximately 25% of all newborns.
Deposition of calcium salts in subcutaneous tissue (i.e., the the lowermost layer of the integument).
The presence of leiomyoma of the skin.
A developmental anomaly characterized by abnormal smallness of both eyes.

An acute condition characterized by sudden visual loss (usually discovered in the morning), optic disc edema at onset, optic disc-related visual field defects. Nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy can be associated with flame hemorrhages on the swollen disk or nearby neuroretinal layer, and sometimes with nearby cotton-wool exudates.
A form of colorblindness in which only two of the three fundamental colors can be distinguished due to a lack of one of the retinal cone pigments.
A usually nonprogressive (i.e., stationary) form of night blindness with early (presumed to be congenital) onset.
Tractional retinal detachment at the periphery of the retina.
Lack of eyelashes on the lower lid.
Congenital abnormality of the extraocular muscles.
A type of cataract with punctate opacities of the lens.
Sharply demarcated, congenital hyperpigmentation of the retinal pigment epithelium. It can be solitary, clustered or multifocal, uni- or bilateral.
A congenital defect of development characterized by absence of the lacrimal gland.
Opacity of the entire lens nucleus.

Degenerative changes of the peripheral retina consisting of close-packed tiny cystic spaces at the outer plexiform/inner nuclear retinal level. The degeneration is common in adult eyes and starts adjacent to the ora serrata and extends circumferentially and posteriorly.

An abnormality of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR). The VOR attempts to keep the image stable on the retina. Ideally passive or active head movements in one direction are compensated for by eye movements of equal magnitude.

Egg yolk-like (vitelliform) maculopathy is a lesion caused by the accumulation of material, often lipofuscin, in the subretinal space underlying the macula. Lesions may be singular or multiple, and may be either sharply or poorly demarcated.
Narrowing of a tear duct (lacrimal duct).
A functional abnormality of the pupil.
Absence of the combined rod-and-cone response on electroretinogram.
An abnormality of the reflex that controls the diameter of the pupil, in response to the intensity of light that falls on the retina of the eye.
Abnormal development (dysgenesis) of the anterior segment of the eye globe. These structures are mainly of mesenchymal origin.
Any deviation from the normal pigmentation of the retina.
Sudden-onset episode of abnormal, involuntary eye movements.
Absence of the crystalline lens of the eye as a result of a developmental defect.
A type of genetically determined disease of the cornea with corneal lesions with a band-like shape.
A malignant melanoma originating within the eye. The tumor originates from the melanocytes in the uvea (which comprises the iris, ciliary body, and choroid).
A chronic irritative conjunctivitis, which commonly presents with general irritation and redness of the eyes, with a burning, dry, or foreign-body sensation of the eyes.

Cornea plana is an abnormally flat shape of the cornea such that the normal protrusion of the cornea from the sclera is missing. The reduced corneal curvature can lead to hyperopia, and a hazy corneal limbus and arcus lipoides may develop at an early age.
Presence of multiple dilatations (sac-like outpouchings) in the blood vessels of the conjunctiva.
A nonspecific term denoting wasting, especially as a result of degeneration, of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
Lack of transparency of the corneal epithelium.
Abnormal (non-physiological) constriction of the pupil of congenital onset.
An abnormal reduction in the amount of pigmentation of the iris.
Abnormal development of the choroid and retina.
Pigment migration into the retina in a bone-spicule configuration (resembling the nucleated cells within the lacuna of bone).
Macular dystrophy is a nonspecific term for retinal degeneration, generally confined to the macula, usually presumed of genetic origin.
Reduced transparency of the stroma of cornea.
A scotoma (area of diminished vision within the visual field) that surrounds the central fixation point.
Localized, irregular dilatation of small tortuous intraretinal blood vessels.
Increased depth of the anterior chamber, i.e., the anteroposterior distance between the cornea and the iris is increased.
Underdevelopment of the optic disc, that is of the optic nerve head, where ganglion cell axons exit the eye to form the optic nerve.
The presence of an increased number of twists and turns of retinal blood vessels (arteries, arterioles, veins, venules).
Progressive loss of peripheral retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and/or neurosensory retinal cells.
An impairment of the ability to track objects with the ocular smooth pursuit system, a class of rather slow eye movements that minimizes retinal target motion.
Ocular abnormality characterized by premature degeneration of the vitreous and the retina that may be associated with increased risk of retinal detachment.
Fibrous connective tissue resulting from incomplete healing of a wound (i.e., a scar) located in the choroid and retina or the eye.
A type of retinal neovascularization that affects the posterior pole of the retina.
A type of cataract characterized by punctate, dust-like opacities within the cortical region of the lens.
A type of cataract affecting the posterior pole of lens immediately adjacent to ('beneath') the Lens capsule.
A nonspecific term denoting wasting, especially as a result of degeneration, of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) that occurs in small, isolated areas.
Mottled (spotted or blotched with different shades) pigmentary abnormality of the macula.
A cataract that affects the anterior part of the cortex of the lens.
A group of development abnormalities of retinal blood vessels.
The presence of whitish deposits in the conjunctiva resembling salt. May be related to calcinosis.
Abnormal largeness of the eye with an axial length > 2.5 standard deviations from population mean.

The presence of central, fine, whitish granular lesions in the stroma of the cornea. This type of corneal dystrophy is usually asymptomatic and begins in childhood and shows a slow progression. Later in the course, the corneal epithelium and Bowman's layer may be affected. Histologically, the cornea shows a uniform deposition of hyaline material.
Complete color blindness, a complete inability to distinguish colors. Affected persons cannot perceive colors, but only shades of gray.
Nystagmus consisting of horizontal to-and-fro eye movements of equal velocity.

The presence of one or more dendritic corneal epithelial ulcers characterized by a treelike branching linear pattern with feathery edges and terminal bulbs. Herpetiform corneal ulcers can be identified by fluorescein staining.
A form of uveitis that is not associated with the formation of granulomas.

Mottling (spots or blotches of different shades) of the retinal pigment epithelium, i.e., localized or generalized fundus pigment granularity associated with processes at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium.

A supranuclear gaze palsy is an inability to look in a horizontal direction as a result of cerebral impairment. There is a loss of the voluntary aspect of eye movements, but, as the brainstem is still intact, all the reflex conjugate eye movements are normal.
The presence of distinct colors in the central (pupillary) zone of the iris than in the mid-peripheral (ciliary) zone.
Presenile cataract is a kind of cataract that occurs in early adulthood, that is, at an age that is younger than usual.
Congenital absence or closure of the opening of the lacrimal punctum.
Paralysis of both the extrinsic and intrinsic ocular muscles.
Inability to see well at night or in poor light with onset in adulthood.

Nonprogressive restriction of movement of the external ocular muscles such that the eyes of affected individuals are partially or completely fixed in a strabismic position. Residual eye movements are significantly limited.
A kind of cataract that progresses with age.
Increased length of the upper eyelashes.
Deposition of hyaline extracellular material (amyloid) into the vitreous humor, which can manifest as vitreous opacities and reduced visual acuity.
Narrowing of the retinal blood vessels, both arterioles and venules.
Punctate opacification (reduced transparency) of the corneal stroma.
Punched out lesions in the pigmented layer of the retina.
Horizontal nystagmus dating from or present at birth.
Deposition of calcium salts in the retina.
Fibrosis of only some of the external ocular muscles such that the eyes of affected individuals are partially or completely fixed in a strabismic position.
Benign choroidal tumour, seen in the fundus as a reddish or orange choroidal lesion and usually associated with cystoid edema, and less commonly with Subretinal fluid.

A shape created by an acute downward arching of the upper eyelid and upward arching of the lower eyelid, toward the medial canthus, which gives the outline of the palpebral fissures the configuration of an almond. Thus, the maximum distance between the fissures is offset from, and medial to, the center point.
Allergic Conjunctivitis is an allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva.
An abnormally slow velocity of horizontal saccadic eye movements.
Congenital absence of the extraocular muscles.
A type of posterior subcapsular cataract characterized by an iridescent color.
Generalized or focal reduced pigmentation of the fundus, evaluated in the context of skin and hair color. Fundoscopy may reveal a low level pigment.
Failure of attachment of the retina during development.
Bleeding within the vitreous compartment of the eye.
Chorioretinal atrophy along the retinal veins.
Intraocular pressure that is 2 standard deviations above the population mean.
A type of of patterned retinal dystrophy that shows a reticular pattern of pigmentation.

This corneal dystrophy affects the posterior limiting membrane of the cornea and is characterized by polymorphous plaques of calcium deposits in the deep stromal layers of the cornea, and occasionally by vesicular lesions of the endothelium and edema of the deep corneal stroma.
A type of retinal detachment arising due to a combination of contracting retinal membranes, abnormal vitreoretinal adhesions, and vitreous changes, in the absence of a full-thickness retinal defect.
Myelinated retinal nerve fiber (MRNF) layer is a rare and mostly benign congenital anomaly in which the retinal nerve fibers anterior to the lamina cribrosa have a myelin sheath.
A congenital defect resulting in absence of the lacrimal duct.
Anomaly of the visual evoked potentials elicited by a flash stimulus, generally a flash of light subtending an angle of at least 20 degrees of the visual field and presented in a dimly lit room.
Separation of the inner layers of the retina (neural retina) from the pigment epithelium occurring near the outer limit (periphery) of the retina.
Congenital abnormal dilation of the pupil on both sides.
Regional increase in the width (height) of the lateral eyebrow.
Fibrosis of the external ocular muscles such that the eyes of affected individuals are partially or completely fixed in a strabismic position. Residual eye movements are significantly limited.
A pattern of peripheral netlike retinal pigmentation that forms a polygonal arrangement of hyperpigmented lines forming geometric patterns in the fundus.
A form of monochromacy in which vision is derived from the remaining preserved blue (S) cones and rod photoreceptors.
Limited mobility of the eye within its socket.
Paralysis of the iris and ciliary apparatus.
A form of stapes ankylosis with congenital onset.
A fixed reduction in the vertical distance between the upper and lower eyelids with short palpebral fissures on one side only.

A subtype of retinitis pigmentosa in which, instead of the pathology starting in the mid-periphery like typical retinitis pigmentosa, the disease starts in the near periphery closer to the vascular arcades and tends to spare the far periphery.
A type of posterior cortical cataract characterized by dense lenticular opacities.
Chorioretinal atrophy concentrated around the optic papilla (i.e., the optic nerve head).

A spectrum of fundoscopic appearances characterized by the development of a variety of patterns of deposits predominantly in the macular area. The deposits are typically bilateral, relatively symmetrical, yellow/white and associated with changes at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium. With time, retinal atrophy may occur. A number of pattern dystrophy subtypes have been described including butterfly-shaped dystrophy, reticular dystrophy (net-like pattern) and fundus pulverulentus (granular, mottled pigmentation).

Persistence of the hyaloid artery, which is the embryonic artery that runs from the optic disc to the posterior lens capsule may persist; the site of attachment may form an opacity. The hyaloid artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery, and usually regresses completely before birth. This features results from a failure of regression of the hyaloid vessel, which supplies the primary vitreous during embryogenesis and normally regresses in the third trimester of pregnancy, leading to a particular form of posterior cataract.
A congenital cataract in which opacity is limited to layers of the lens external to the nucleus (i.e., the perinuclear region), i.e., between the nuclear and cortical layers of the lens.
Abnormal growth and differentiation, structure and appearance of the retina present from birth.
Saccadic undershoot of horizontal saccadic eye movements, i.e., a horizontal saccadic eye movement that has less than the magnitude that would be required to gain fixation of the object.

Cerulean cataracts are a kind of congenital cataract having peripheral bluish and white opacifications in concentric layers with occasional central lesions arranged radially. Although the opacities may be observed during fetal development and childhood, usually visual acuity is only mildly reduced until adulthood, when lens extraction is generally necessary.
Horizontal nystagmus made apparent by looking to the right or to the left.
Discrete areas of pallor in which the pigment epithelium, choriocapillaris and choroidal pigment are absent.
A dark-adapted bright flash electroretinogram in which the b-wave that is of markedly lower amplitude than the associated a-wave.
Blockage of retinal arteriole, generally associated with interruption of blood flow and oxygen delivery to affected regions of the retina. This can affect the inner or mid-retinal structures.
Decreased amount of pigmentation in the macula.
Retinal exudate within the retinal tissue itself.
Underdevelopment of the stroma of iris.
A pattern of white lines and dots in the far periphery of the retina.
Congenital malformation of the lacrimal duct associated with incomplete development of the bony nasolacrimal canal or craniofacial anomalies.
Loss of peripheral vision with retention of central vision, resulting in a constricted circular tunnel-like field of vision.

An abnormally reduced response to stimulation of the cornea (by touch, foreign body, blowing air). The corneal reflex (also known as the blink reflex, normally results in an involuntary blinking of the eyelids.
Increased amount of pigmentation in the fovea.
Any deviation from the normal, uniform distribution or appearance of pigment within the macular region of the retina.
Reduced transparency of the peripheral region of the cornea.
Partial dislocation of the lens in a superior direction.
A form of macular degeneration characterized by the presence of multiple cystoid spaces in the macula.
A type of sutural cataract in which the opacity follows the posterior Y suture.

Retinitis pigmentosa inversa is form of retinal degeneration characterized by areas of retinal/chorioretinal degeneration with pigment migration in the macular area (in contrast to retinitis pigmentosa which, at early disease stages, predominantly affects the retinal periphery).
Absence of the anterior chamber of the eye owing to a developmental defect.
Absence or underdevelopment of the lacrimal gland.
Focal decreased retinal arteriolar diameters, which may decrease blood flow and slow oxygen delivery to regions of the retina.
A structural abnormality of retinal vasculature.
An abnormality of the line of Schwalbe.
An abnormality of an extraocular muscle.
An anomaly of the space between the medial and lateral canthi of the two open eyelids.
A wrinkle of retinal tissue projecting outward from the surface of the retina and visible as a line on fundoscopy.
Absence or underdevelopment of the iris.
Any abnormality of the blood vessels of the conjunctiva.
Absence or underdevelopment of the uvea, the pigmented middle layer of the eye consisting of the iris and ciliary body together with the choroid.
A developmental defect characterized by lack of development or underdevelopment of the fundus/fovea.
Congenital absence or underdevelopment of the fovea.
Absence or underdevelopment of the anterior segment of the eye.
Absence or underdevelopment of the lens.
An abnormality of the skin characterized the presence of excessive amounts of dry surface scales on the skin resulting from an abnormality of keratinization.
The presence of one or more bullae on the skin, defined as fluid-filled blisters more than 5 mm in diameter with thin walls.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the skin.
Increased blood pressure during a pregnancy.
Virilization (deepening of voice, facial hirsutism and scalp hair loss) with onset during pregnancy (usually towards the end of the first trimester) and regression several months post-partum.
An abnormally low concentration of serum conjugated estriol as compared to normal values for gestational-age.
Reduction in bone mineral density affecting any or all of the tarsal bones, seven bones of the foot comprising the calcaneus, talus, cuboid, navicular, and the cuneiform bones.
A developmental abnormality characterized by the absence of the fifth metatarsal bone.
Medial deviation of the great toe owing to a deformity of the great toe joint causing the hallux to deviate medially.
An outward deviation of the foot at the talocalcaneal or subtalar joint.
The presence of a fifth metatarsal bone that has not undergone ossification at an age when ossification is usually visible.
An anomaly of the fifth metatarsal bone.
An overall widening of the spaces between the digits.
Medial deviation of the second toe.
Delayed maturation and calcification of any of the tarsal bones, seven bones of the foot comprising the calcaneus, talus, cuboid, navicular, and the cuneiform bones.
The presence of unusually deep creases (ridges/wrinkles) on the skin of sole of foot located between the first and second toe.
Precocious (accelerated) maturation and calcification of any of the tarsal bones, seven bones of the foot comprising the calcaneus, talus, cuboid, navicular, and the cuneiform bones.
A type of contracture in which the plantar flexion muscles are contracted.
Osteosclerosis of the endosteal surface of the diaphyses (shafts) of the metatarsal bones.
Bending or curvature of a third toe in the tibial direction (i.e., towards the big toe).
Limitation of the ability to bend the toes.
Synostosis of the calcaneus with the navicular bone.
A congenital deformity characterized by a dorsiflexed, inverted, and adducted foot, i.e., a combination of talipes calcaneus and talipes varus.
A two-part calcaneus, a finding that probably results from delayed coalescence of two primary calcaneal centers of ossification.
The presence of abnormal punctate (speckled, dot-like) calcifications in one or more tarsal bones.

Hindfoot valgus (posterior part of the foot turns outward) in combination with forefoot abduction (front part of the foot (the forefoot) is angled outwards away from the midline of the body, relative to the hindfoot) and lowering of the midfoot.
Defective ossification in an irregular pattern of the seven bones of the foot comprising the calcaneus, talus, cuboid, navicular, and the cuneiform bones.

Abnormal plantar flexion of the calcaneus relative to the longitudinal axis of the tibia. This results in the angle between the long axis of the tibia and the long axis of the heel bone (calcaneus) being greater than 90 degrees.
Delayed maturation and calcification of the calcaneus.
Abnormal response to epinephrine as manifested by reduced or lacking aggregation of platelets upon addition of epinephrine.
Elevations of the levels of SGOT (serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase) and SGPT (serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase) that occur during infections.

Increased time to coagulation in the prothrombin time test, which is a measure of the extrinsic pathway of coagulation. The results of the prothrombin time test are often expressed in terms of the International normalized ratio (INR), which is calculated as a ratio of the patient's prothrombin time (PT) to a control PT standardized for the potency of the thromboplastin reagent developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) using the formula: INR is equal to Patient PT divided by Control PT.
Episodes of muscle weakness associated with reduced levels of potassium in the blood.
Excessive amounts of mucopolysaccharide in the urine.
Hyperapobetalipoproteinemia is defined as the combination of a normal low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol in the face of an increased LDL apolipoprotein B (apoB) protein.
The concentration of 2-hydroxydicarboxylic acid in the urine, normalized for urine concentration, is above the upper limit of normal.
Alkaline phosphatase levels measured within leukocytes is below detectable levels.
An increased concentration of ammonia in the blood not associated with symptoms such as encephalopathy.
Abnormally reduced concentration of cortisol in the blood.
Abnormally decreased rate of beta-galactosidase activity. Beta-galactosidase activity can be measured in leukocyte, fibroblast, or plasma.

Reduced activity of coagulation factor VII. Factor VII is part of the extrinsic coagulation pathway, which is initiated at the site of injury in response to the release of tissue factor (fIII). Tissue factor and activated factor VII catalyze the activation of factor X.
An abnormal reduction in the Arden ratio, which is the ratio between the light peak and the dark trough of the smoothed (physiologic) EOG record.
An absence of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol in the blood.
The onset of puberty before the age of 9 years in boys.
The presence of large polyhedral cells with eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and enlarged nuclei in the adrenal cortex.
No secondary sexual characteristics are present at puberty.

Thyroid dysgenesis is a descriptive term that should be avoided if more precise information is available. However, the HPO keeps retains this term because it is commonly used in the medical literature. In humans, the process of thyroid morphogenesis occurs from the 3rd to 16th week of gestation. Alterations occurring during this period may result in a thyroid gland that is absent (thyroid agenesis or athyreosis), hypoplastic (thyroid hypoplasia), or located in an unusual position (thyroid ectopy). All these entities are grouped under the term thyroid dysgenesis.
The congenital absence of the thyroid gland.
The presence of multiple pancreatic islet cell adenomas.
Deficiency of parathyroid hormone with congenital onset.
A type of hyperparathyroidism caused by a primary abnormality of the parathyroid glands (e.g., adenoma, carcinoma, hyperplasia). Primary hyperparathyroidism is associated with hyercalcemia.

A reduced level of prolactin in the blood circulation. Prolactin is a protein hormone that is secreted by lactotrophs in the anterior pituitary and that stimulates mammary gland development and milk production.
Ketosis-resistant diabetes is a synonym for type II diabetes. This term thus refers to a form of type II diabetes in which patients are dependent on insulin.
Insufficient production of steroid hormones (primarily cortisol) by the adrenal glands as a result of a primary defect in the glands themselves.

Amenorrhea due to loss of ovarian function before the age of 40. Primary ovarian insuficiency (POI) is a state of female hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. It can manifest as primary amenorrhea with onset before menarche or secondary amenorrhea.

A reduced ability to secrete gonadotropins, which are protein hormones secreted by gonadotrope cells of the anterior pituitary gland, including the hormones follitropin (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH).
A reduction below normal concentration of estradiol in the circulation.
Abnormal development of the adrenal gland.
Condition associated with a raised serum concentration of thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) but a normal serum free thyroxine (FT4).

A condition in which the pituitary gland is partially resistant to thyroid hormone, so that it continues to secrete thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) until the blood level of thyroid hormone rises higher than normal.
The presence of lymphangiectasis of the thyroid gland.
An elevated concentration of follicle-stimulating hormone in the blood.
An reduced concentration of progesterone in the blood.
A type of hypothyroidism that results from a defect in thyrotropin-releasing hormone activity.
Developmental hypoplasia of the adrenal medulla.
A state of renal tubular unresponsiveness or resistance to the action of aldosterone.
A type of adrenal hypoplasia with congenital onset.
A type of hypothyroidism that results from a defect in thyroid-stimulating hormone secretion.
Increased levels of thyroxine without evidence of clinical thyroid disease.
An enlargement of the thyroid gland with congenital onset.
Adrenocortical adenomas are benign tumors of the adrenal cortex.
A type of adrenal hyperplasia with congenital onset.
Adrenal insufficiency secondary to a defect in the ACTH receptor.
The presence of an adenoma of the pancreas with origin in a pancreatic B cell.

The presence of intracellular inclusion bodies (aggregates of stainable substances, usually proteins) in neutrophils. Cytoplasmic neutrophil inclusions (oval, basophilic) are also known as Doehle bodies.

Abnormal morphology of collagen fibers in cartilage. In cartilage, collagen II, actually a collagen II:IX:XI heterofibril, is by far the most important type of collagen. A number of abnormalities may be appreciated by electron micrography or biochemical investigations, including sparse collagen fibers in the cartilage matrix.
An abnormality of zinc ion homeostasis.
An increased concentration of ammonia in the blood with sudden onset.
An increased amount of unconjugated (indirect) bilurubin in the blood.
An increased concentration of insulin in the blood in the fasting state, i.e., not as the response to food intake.
A partial reduction in level of the complement component Factor H in circulation.
A type of pituitary adenoma that produces adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH).
An increase in the level of long-chain dicarboxylic acid in the urine.

A condition of not having consistently high levels of phenylalanine in the blood but of experiencing temporary hyperphenylalaninemia following ingestion of large quantities of phenylalanine (for instance, following an oral loading test with phenylalanine).
An increased concentration of dermatan sulfate in the urine.
Degeneration of the olivary bodies, prominent oval structures in the medulla oblongata.
Presence of myoglobin in the urine following exercise.
An increase in the level of medium chain dicarboxylic acid in the urine.
Lower than normal amount of myelin in the dorsal (posterior) tract of the spinal cord white matter.
A reduction in the activity of the mitochondrial respiratory chain complex II, which is part of the electron transport chain in mitochondria.
A decreased concentration of free (unbound) carnitine in the blood.
An abnormality of the mitochondria in muscle tissue.
Increased alkaline phosphatase measured within leukocytes.
Abnormal response to collagen or collagen-mimetics as manifested by reduced or lacking aggregation of platelets upon addition collagen or collagen-mimetics.

Reduced activity of coagulation factor X. The extrinsic and intrinsic pathways converge at factor X (fX). The extrinsic pathway activates fX by means of d factor VII with its cofactor, tissue factor. The intrinsic pathway activates fX by means of the tenase complex (Ca2+ and factors VIIIa, IXa and X) on the surface of activated platelets. Factor Xa in turn activates prothrombin (factor II) to thrombin (factor IIa).
Any structural anomaly of the mitochondria.
An abnormality of the combined rod-and-cone response on electroretinogram.
An abnormally decreased concentration of vitamin B6 in the blood circulation.
The presence of microscopic crystalline calcium precipitates in the form of oxalate and/or phosphate in the renal parenchyma.
Decreased activity of von Willebrand factor. Von Willebrand factor mediates the adhesion of platelets to the collagen exposed on endothelial cell surfaces.
A partial reduction in level of the complement component Factor D in circulation.
An increased urine level of any amino acid carrying two amino groups (Asparagine, glutamine and lysine, cystine, ornithine).

A type of renal tubular acidosis characterized by a failure of acid secretion by the alpha intercalated cells of the cortical collecting duct of the distal nephron. The urine cannot be acidified below a pH of 5.3, associated with acidemia and hypokalemia.
Concentration of a branched chain amino acid in the blood above the upper limit of normal.
A reduction in the activity of the mitochondrial respiratory chain complex IV, which is part of the electron transport chain in mitochondria.
A reduction in immunoglobulin levels of the IgG2 subclass in the blood circulation.

An abnormality of adhesion of thrombocytes. Normally, platelets adhere to collagen in the vascular subendothelium within seconds of injury via a receptor made up of glycoprotein Ia and IIa and GPVI and to vWF via receptor GPIb/IX/V. The adherent platelets then release granules that lead to platelet activation and aggregation.

The presence of an abnormally increased concentration of neutral amino acids in the urine. The neutral amino acids are tryptophan, alanine, asparagine, glutamine, histidine, isoleucine, leucine, phenylalanine, serine, threonine, tyrosine and valine.
Reduced ability to transform factor X into its activated form factor Xa.
Decreased activity of coagulation factor XIII (also known as fibrin stabilizing factor). Activated Factor XIII cross-links fibrin polymers solidifying the clot.
An increased concentration of proline in the blood.
A neonatal decreased concentration of proteins in the blood.
Absence or underdevelopment of the big toe.
Absence or underdevelopment of the tarsal bones.
An abnormality of the calcaneus, also known as the heel bone, one of the or heel bone, one of the components of the tarsus of the foot which make up the heel.
Contractures of one or more joints of the feet meaning chronic loss of joint motion due to structural changes in non-bony tissue.
Synostosis (bony fusion) involving one or more bones of the tarsus (calcaneus, talus, cuboid, navicular, cuneiiform bones).
An abnormality of the formation and mineralization of any of the tarsal bones, seven bones of the foot comprising the calcaneus, talus, cuboid, navicular, and the cuneiform bones.

Any abnormal process of ossification of the metatarsal bones, which normally are each ossified from two centers: one for the body, and one for the head (metatarsal II,III,IV, and V) and one for the body and one for the base (metatarsal I). The ossification process begins in the center of the body about the ninth week, and extends toward either extremity. The center for the base of the first metatarsal appears about the third year, and the centers for the heads of the other bones between the fifth and eighth years. They join the bodies between the eighteenth and twentieth years.
Concentration of vitamin A in the blood circulation outside limits of normal.
Nails whose growth is slower than normal.
Aplasia or developmental hypoplasia of the nail.
Repeated loss, or shedding, of the nails of the fingers and toes.
The presence of misshapen or partially destroyed nail plates, often with accumulation of soft, yellow keratin between the dystrophic nail plate and nail bed, resulting in elevation of the nail plate.
A thickening of the stratum corneum in the region beneath the nails.
Chronic infection of the nails by Candida species.
A nail of the fifth finger that is diminished in length and width, i.e., underdeveloped nail of little finger.
A thickening of the stratum corneum, the outer layer of the skin, in the region surrounding the nails.
Detachment of the distal fingernails from the nail bed.
Longitudinal, linear prominences in the fingernail plate.

Onychodystrophy (nail dystrophy) refers to nail changes apart from changes of the color (nail dyschromia) and involves partial or complete disruption of the various keratinous layers of the nail plate.
The presence of degenerative changes of intervertebral disk.
The presence of punctiform calcification of the bone of the vertebral bodies.
An abnormal shape of the vertebral bodies whereby the vertebral bodies are thick on one side and taper to a thin edge at the other.
The presence of developmental dysplasia of the vertebral column.
Schisis (cleft or cleavage) of vertebral bodies.
Anterior tongue-like protrusions of the vertebral bodies of the lumbar spine.
An abnormality of the shape of the lumbar vertebra L1 such that it is wedge-shaped (narrow towards the front).
A morphological abnormality of the vertebral arch, i.e., of the posterior part of a vertebra.
Absence of one half of the vertebral body in the lumbar spine.
Any abnormality of the atlas and the axis.
The presence of one or more herniated nucleus pulposus of intervertebral disk.
Excessive growth of the bones of the vertebral bodies.

A progressive disorder of vertebral joint degeneration that occurs in the setting of any condition characterized by decreased afferent innervation, involving loss of deep pain and proprioceptive sensation in the vertebral column. Patients most commonly present with symptoms of lower back pain, sitting imbalance, progressive spinal deformity (usually kyphosis), and an audible clicking sound on changing postures.
An abnormality of the shape of vertebrae, such that they are wedge-shaped (narrow towards the back).
An abnormal narrowing of the cervical spinal canal.

A reduction of the distance between vertebral pedicles, which are the two short, thick processes, which project backward, one on either side, from the upper part of the vertebral body, at the junction of its posterior and lateral surfaces.
Over curvature of the lumbar region.

A developmental defect of the sacrum characterized by partial or disordered development of the sacrum in which portions of the sacrum, which normally is formed by fusion of five sacral vertebrae S1-S5, fail to form or fail to form normally.
A partial dislocation of the intervertebral joint between the second and third cervical vertebrae.

Narrowing (becoming gradually narrower) of the distance between vertebral pedicles that gets progressively more severe towards to caudal (lower) end of the vertebral column. Note that normally, the interpedicular distances get progressively wider as one proceeds down the spine.
A progressive form of scoliosis with congenital onset.
Agenesis of one or more vertebrae of the cervical vertebral column.
A developmental defect characterized by agenesis of one or more vertebral bodies.
Absence of one half of the vertebral body in the thoracic spine.
An abnormality related to a defect of vertebral separation of sacral vertebrae during development.
Dysplasia of the cervical vertebral column.
A reduction of the distance between the lower thoracic vertebral pedicles.
An abnormal reduction of the anterioposterior diameter of the vertebral body.
Decreased ossification of the cervical vertebral bodies, i.e., of the Cervical vertebrae set.
Arthrosis, i.e., of degenerative joint disease, affecting the cervical vertebral column.
A reduction of the distance between thoracolumbar vertebral pedicles.
Narrowing (becoming gradually narrower) of the distance between lumbar vertebral pedicles that gets progressively more severe towards to caudal (lower) end of the vertebral column.
Complete bilateral fractures of the pars interarticularis resulting in the anterior slippage of the fifth lumbar vertebral body (L5) onto the sacrum (level S1).
Early closure (ossification) of the anterior fontanelle, which generally undergoes closure around the 18th month of life.
Partial displacement of the lens in the inferior direction.
A severe form of hypermetropia with over +5.00 diopters.
The presence of a moderate form of sensorineural hearing impairment.
Reduced transparency of the central posterior portion of the corneal stroma.
A bilateral type of conductive hearing impairment.
Aplasia or developmental hypoplasia of the sacral bone.
Any structural abnormality of the coccyx.
Permanent indentation on the posteromedial aspect of the helix that may be sharply or indistinctly delineated.
A type of hearing impairment caused by an abnormal functionality of the cochlear nerve with congenital onset.
Absence of the acoustic reflex, an involuntary contraction of the stapedius muscle that occurs in response to high-intensity sound stimuli.
A type of hearing impairment affecting primarily the low frequencies of sound (125 Hz to 1000 Hz).
Any structural anomaly of the border of the helix, which usually forms a rolled rim but is highly variable in shape.
The presence of a malformed cochlea.
Complete lack of functioning of the vestibular apparatus.
